body_markdown:
Consumers across the UK are being urged to check their fridges and cupboards after four wrap products were recalled over concerns about the possible presence of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, also known as STEC.


Summit Foods has issued a recall covering several popular chicken wrap products, while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) has advised customers who have purchased the affected products not to eat them.


The recall is an important reminder of why consumers should pay close attention to food safety notices, product labels and use-by dates.


## Which Wrap Products Have Been Recalled?


The recall affects four products supplied by Summit Foods. The products named in the food safety warning are:


- Snacksters Chicken Fajita Wrap
- Snacksters Hoi Sin Wrap
- East Street Deli Sweet Chilli Chicken Wrap
- Target a Snack Chicken Fajita Wrap


The affected products are subject to the recall because of the possible presence of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.


According to the information reported in the recall notice, the warning applies to products with use-by dates up to and including **September 5, 2026** . Consumers who have any of the affected products should check the packaging carefully before deciding what to do with them.


The Snacksters Chicken Fajita Wrap was being sold through Iceland and Bestway Wholesale, according to the published information.


## What Should Consumers Do With the Recalled Wraps?


The Food Standards Agency has advised consumers not to eat any affected products.


If you have purchased one of the recalled wraps, the safest course of action is to avoid consuming it and dispose of the product.


Summit Foods has also advised customers to provide proof of purchase by contacting the company atsales@summitfoods.co.uk , including information about when and where the product was purchased, if they are seeking a refund.


Consumers should not assume that cooking or reheating a recalled product makes it safe. When an official food recall has been issued, following the instructions provided by the manufacturer and food safety authorities is the appropriate response.


## What Is E. coli?


E. coli is a type of bacteria that can be found in a variety of environments, including food, water and the intestines of people and animals.


Not all E. coli bacteria are dangerous. Many types are harmless and form part of the normal intestinal bacteria found in healthy people.


However, some strains can cause serious illness. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC, is one type that can result in significant gastrointestinal symptoms.


The FSA says symptoms can include severe diarrhoea, which may sometimes be bloody, as well as abdominal pain.


In some cases, STEC infection can develop into haemolytic uremic syndrome, commonly known as HUS. This is a serious condition that can lead to kidney failure and can be fatal.


## E. coli Symptoms to Watch For


People who may have consumed a recalled product should be aware of possible symptoms.


Symptoms associated with STEC can include:


- Severe diarrhoea
- Bloody diarrhoea
- Abdominal pain
- Symptoms associated with haemolytic uremic syndrome in more serious cases


Anyone who develops concerning symptoms after eating a recalled food should seek appropriate medical advice.


The FSA has also advised that people experiencing symptoms should stay away from work, school or nursery until they have been free from symptoms for at least 48 hours. This is intended to reduce the risk of spreading infection to other people.


## Who May Be More Vulnerable to Severe E. coli Illness?


While anyone can potentially become unwell from harmful E. coli strains, some groups can face a greater risk of serious complications.


The source information identifies children under five, adults over 65 and people with weakened immune systems among those who may be particularly vulnerable.


This makes it especially important for households with young children, older adults or vulnerable family members to check whether they have any recalled products stored at home.


Food recalls can sometimes be overlooked because packaging may look normal and a product may have been purchased days or weeks earlier. Checking the product name and use-by date is therefore an important step when a recall is announced.


## Why Food Recalls Matter


Food recalls are issued when a potential safety problem is identified with a product. In this case, Summit Foods is taking precautionary action because of the possible presence of STEC.


Consumers may see recall notices in shops, on retailer websites or through official food safety announcements.


A food recall does not necessarily mean that every individual product is contaminated. However, consumers should follow the recall instructions when a particular product and date range has been identified.


The safest approach is not to take unnecessary risks with recalled food.


## How to Stay Safe During a Food Recall


When a food recall is announced, consumers can take several simple steps.


First, check your fridge, freezer and cupboards for the affected product. Compare the exact product name and use-by date with the recall information.


Second, do not consume a product that falls within the affected recall information.


Third, follow the manufacturer's instructions regarding disposal and refunds.


Finally, keep an eye on official food safety announcements for updates. Recall information can change as investigations continue, and additional products may sometimes be identified.


Good food hygiene practices are also important. Washing hands regularly, keeping raw and ready-to-eat foods separate and cleaning food preparation surfaces can all help reduce the risk of foodborne illness.


## The Latest UK Wrap Recall Explained


The recall of four wrap products highlights the importance of checking food safety notices, particularly when buying ready-to-eat foods.


Summit Foods has recalled the Snacksters Chicken Fajita Wrap, Snacksters Hoi Sin Wrap, East Street Deli Sweet Chilli Chicken Wrap and Target a Snack Chicken Fajita Wrap because of the possible presence of STEC.


The FSA has advised consumers not to eat affected products and to dispose of them instead.


Anyone who has symptoms associated with STEC should take appropriate medical advice. People who are experiencing symptoms should also follow public health guidance about staying away from work, school or nursery for at least 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.


For consumers, the key message is simple: **check your products, do not eat recalled wraps and follow official food safety guidance.**


### Source


The **Daily Mirror** on August 21, 2026.

This article is provided for general information only and is based on the source material available at the time of writing. It is not medical advice and should not be used as a substitute for advice from a qualified healthcare professional or official food safety authority. Product recalls and safety guidance can change, so readers should check the latest information from the Food Standards Agency and the relevant manufacturer or retailer.
